## Heal Selection

Heal Selection takes something out of a photo by filling the selected area with image from around it: a speck of dust, a scratch, a power line, a small object on grass, sand, sky or a wall. It runs on your Mac, needs no key and costs nothing.

1. Select what should go, with any selection tool. Cover the whole object, shadow included, but keep close to it; Glimmer grows the selection by 3 pixels by itself, so the object's edge goes too. If part of the object is left outside, the fill continues it.
2. Choose **Edit › Heal Selection**, or click **Heal** (the bandage) in the selection bar.

The fill lands in a new layer named **Heal**, above the active layer and holding only the filled area, so the photo underneath is unchanged. Hide or delete the layer to get the object back. The whole thing is one undo step, and the selection stays, so you can undo, adjust the selection and try again. A feathered selection gives a softer join.

Heal Selection copies what is already in the photo. It does not invent anything. Glimmer looks at the image just around the area and picks one of two ways to fill it:

- An area that is very thin, or that sits on an even surface, is filled smoothly from its edges inward.
- An area on a textured surface is filled piece by piece with small patches copied from the surroundings, starting where lines and edges run into the area so that they continue across it.

What to expect depends on how wide the area is at its thickest. A long power line 6 pixels thick counts as 6 pixels, however long it is.

| Width at the thickest | Result |
|---|---|
| Up to about 120 px | Usually good on sky, water, grass, sand, wood, walls and similar. About a second. |
| 120 to 250 px | Glimmer asks first. The fill may smear or show repeats. Several seconds. |
| Over 250 px | Not filled. Use Remove Object instead. |

It works less well where fine detail crosses the area, such as branches against a cloud or the edge between two different surfaces: the fill then picks one of them and the detail is lost. So heal a long thing in sections. For a power line, select and heal the stretch across the sky first, then the stretch across the cloud, and leave the short part that crosses a tree top for the Clone Stamp or for Remove Object. For a large object, or one in front of a complicated scene, use **AI › Remove Object**, which generates new image and needs an OpenRouter key (see [AI with OpenRouter](11-ai-with-openrouter.md)).

Heal Selection reads everything that is visible, so it works whatever kind of layer is active. A progress entry with a Cancel button shows in the AI panel's job list while it runs; cancelling leaves the document as it was.

## Photoshop files

Glimmer opens Photoshop files (PSD, and the large-document form PSB) with their layers, as a new, untitled Glimmer document. The Photoshop file itself is never changed. Open one with **File › Open…** or by dragging it onto Glimmer.

What comes through as it was, for RGB and grayscale files with 8 or 16 bits per channel:

- Layers of pixels, with their names, positions, transparency, opacity and visibility.
- Groups, open or closed, and clipping.
- Layer masks, including masks that are switched off.
- The blend modes Glimmer has, which is all of Photoshop's except Dissolve, Darker Color and Lighter Color.
- Solid colour fill layers, and shapes filled with one colour: they come in as fill layers with their outline, which you can go on editing.
- Levels, Curves and Invert adjustment layers. A Curves layer has the same points; between the points the curve may run a little differently than in Photoshop, and the report says so.

The document is set to blend colours the way Photoshop does (**Image › Blend Colors in Gamma Space**), so that half-transparent layers look as they did.

What does not come through in this version, and what happens instead:

- **Text** becomes a layer of pixels with the same name. The words can't be edited as text; the report quotes them.
- **Smart objects** become pixels. The file that was placed in them is not kept.
- The other **adjustment layers**, **gradient and pattern fills**, and shapes with an inverted outline are left out.
- **Layer effects** such as shadows, strokes and glows, and **vector masks**, are not read.
- A layer in one of the three missing **blend modes** comes in as Normal.
- Files in **other colour modes** (CMYK, Lab, indexed colour, duotone, multichannel, bitmap) and files with **32 bits per channel** open as one layer: the flattened picture saved in the file, converted to RGB by macOS. Their layers are not read.

Nothing is dropped silently. When the file has opened, an **Import Report** lists, layer by layer, what did not come through and what was done instead; if everything came through, it says so in one line. Glimmer also compares its own picture of the layers with the flattened picture that the file carries, and the report says whether they match or how much they differ. The report is saved with the Glimmer document: **File › Import Report…** shows it again, also after you have closed and reopened the document.

A file larger than Glimmer's limit for your Mac is refused, with the same message as for other images. A damaged file is refused with a reason rather than opened in part.

Glimmer reads these files with its own code, written from Adobe's published description of the format. It has been tried with files that Glimmer's own tests generate, not yet with files saved by Photoshop. Glimmer does not write Photoshop files yet.
